title:
Viscosity Is Not Flow
Dr. Moh Kolbehdari
gist: A SemiWiki materials-science essay argues that viscosity (resistance to deformation) and flow (actual material motion under pressure, capillary force, or geometry) are distinct in chip packaging, and that the manufactured bond-line or underfill geometry produced by flow — not the viscosity number itself — is what ultimately determines thermal resistance, warpage, yield, and reliability.

themes.theme: Viscosity vs. flow, the core distinction

insights.claim: Viscosity is a material's resistance to deformation, while flow is the actual motion that occurs when pressure, capillary force, gravity, or a moving boundary acts on that material inside a specific package geometry; the two are not the same thing.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Packaging engineers should stop treating a viscosity spec as a proxy for how a material will actually behave in the process; the driving mechanism and geometry must be evaluated separately.
insights.quote: So viscosity does not create flow.

insights.claim: A high-viscosity material can still flow readily if driving pressure is large enough, while a low-viscosity material may barely move without a pressure gradient, capillary force, gravity, or moving boundary, so viscosity alone cannot predict process outcomes.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Do not select or qualify packaging materials on viscosity number alone; test flow behavior under the actual process pressure and geometry conditions.
insights.quote: A high-viscosity material may still flow if the driving pressure is sufficiently large.
insights.locator: Viscosity Is a Property, Not Motion

insights.claim: Different chip-packaging steps rely on distinct physical driving mechanisms: capillary pressure drives capillary underfill (CUF) beneath the die, mold pressure drives molded underfill (MUF), dispensing pressure moves TIM through a syringe, and clamping pressure spreads TIM between surfaces.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Model each packaging step's flow physics separately rather than applying one generic viscosity-flow assumption across CUF, MUF, dispense, and clamp operations.

insights.claim: The same material can exhibit very different flow behavior across dispensing, capillary filling, compression, and thermal cycling because each process step imposes a different driving mechanism and boundary condition.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Flow qualification data from one process step should not be assumed to transfer to predict a material's behavior in a different process step.
insights.quote: The same material can therefore exhibit very different flow behaviour in dispensing, capillary filling, compression, and thermal cycling.

insights.claim: Many thermal interface materials (TIMs), adhesives, and underfills are non-Newtonian, meaning their apparent viscosity changes with shear rate, temperature, filler loading, particle alignment, cure progression, and material history, so a single datasheet viscosity value may not represent what the material actually experiences during the real packaging process.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Treat datasheet viscosity numbers skeptically when evaluating packaging materials; demand process-condition-specific rheology data instead.
insights.quote: the value measured in a material datasheet may not represent the viscosity experienced during the actual package process.

insights.claim: TIM behavior forms a closed feedback loop: temperature and shear history alter apparent viscosity, clamping pressure and gap geometry drive material movement, the resulting flow sets bond-line thickness and void distribution, that geometry determines thermal resistance, and thermal resistance in turn changes temperature, feeding back into material behavior.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Thermal design and reliability modeling for TIM should be treated as a coupled feedback system rather than a one-way calculation from viscosity to thermal resistance.
insights.quote: This is a true coupled loop, but every term still has a distinct physical meaning.

themes.theme: Underfill fill dynamics and the heating trade-off

insights.claim: In capillary underfill (CUF), fill rate depends on surface energy and wetting, gap and stand-off geometry, viscosity, temperature, filler size and concentration, bump-array resistance, dispense pattern, and cure timing, not viscosity alone.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Underfill yield and void risk should be modeled across this full parameter set rather than tuned by adjusting viscosity alone.

insights.claim: Raising temperature to lower underfill viscosity is a double-edged tactic: it can initially improve flow but also accelerates cure, which shortens the available fill window and raises the risk of incomplete fill or premature gelation.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: When tuning dispense temperature for underfill, balance flow-window gains against cure-acceleration risk rather than assuming hotter always means better flow.
insights.quote: Heating therefore may initially improve flow while eventually shortening the available fill window.

insights.claim: The common shorthand that lower viscosity improves underfill flow is an oversimplification; whether the die fills completely without voids, filler filtering, or premature gelation depends on the complete combined process, not viscosity reduction alone.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Flag any single-variable claim about underfill flow improvement as incomplete; verify against the full mechanism stack (wetting, geometry, temperature, filler, cure timing).

insights.claim: The flow process permanently encodes itself into package geometry (local thickness variation, voids, filler segregation, fillet shape, cure shrinkage, residual stress), and that resulting geometry, not the original fluid mechanics, subsequently governs thermal resistance, warpage, interconnect stress, delamination, thermal-cycle fatigue, yield, and lifecycle reliability.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Trace reliability and yield failures back to the specific flow/cure process step that set the geometry, since the process itself is transient but its geometric and stress consequences persist for the product's operating life.
insights.quote: The process may be temporary, but the geometry and stress state it creates remain throughout the product lifecycle.
